# Education in New Zealand
Education in New Zealand encompasses early childhood, primary, secondary, and tertiary levels, governed by a history of both Māori and European influences. Early Māori education centered around wānanga and tohunga elders, passing down tribal knowledge orally within chiefly families. European-style schooling began in 1815, initially focused on teaching in Māori and later shifting to English instruction, establishing a free, compulsory, and secular national education system from 1878 onwards. Today, early childhood education includes teacher-led services (kindergarten, puna reo, ECE centres) and parent-led or culturally-focused services (Kohanga Reo, Playcentre), all following the Te Whāriki curriculum and regulated by the Ministry of Education.
Primary and secondary education is free and compulsory between ages 6 and 16, with most children starting school at age 5 and continuing to age 17. There are 13 school year levels, divided into primary (Years 1–8; Years 7–8 may be at primary, intermediate, or combined schools) and secondary (Years 9–13). The curriculum, set by the NZ Curriculum (English-medium) and Te Marautanga o Aotearoa (Māori-medium), covers eight learning areas, with NCEA as the predominant qualification at senior levels. Education takes place in state schools (85% of students), state-integrated schools (10%), and private schools (4%), as well as alternatives like home-schooling and, formerly, charter schools now state-integrated. Māori language education ranges from full immersion (Kura Kaupapa Māori) to Māori language classes within English-medium schools. Tertiary education is offered through universities and vocational institutions, funded by a mixture of government subsidies and student fees, with access to student loans and allowances.
Funding for schools is determined by student numbers, socio-economic status, and additional support for low-decile and special needs students. School enrolment mostly operates based on geographic zones, with open and limited-enrolment schemes in place to manage student distribution. New Zealand schools generally face challenges in numeracy and literacy standards, bullying, and equitable outcomes for Māori and Pacific students, with ongoing reforms and targeted Māori-medium education helping close achievement gaps and improve educational outcomes for all.
